/-!
# Erdős Problem 1159

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/1159](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1159)
- [ESS83] Erdős, P. and Silverman, R. and Stein, A., *Intersection properties of families containing
  sets of nearly the same size*. Ars Combin. (1983), 247--259.
- [Er81] Erdős, P., *On the combinatorial problems which I would most like to see solved*.
  Combinatorica (1981), 25-42.
-/

@[expose] public section

open Configuration

namespace Erdos1159

/--
Determine whether there exists a constant $C>1$ such that the following holds.

Let $P$ be a finite [projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane). Must there exist a set of points $S$ such that $1\leq \lvert S\cap \ell\rvert \leq C$ for all lines $\ell$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 51]
theorem erdos_1159 : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ C : ℕ, 1 < C ∧
      ∀ (P L : Type) (_ : Membership P L) (_ : Fintype P) (_ : Fintype L),
        ∀ _ : ProjectivePlane P L, ∃ S : Set P, ∀ l : L,
          1 ≤ (S ∩ {p : P | p ∈ l}).ncard ∧ (S ∩ {p : P | p ∈ l}).ncard ≤ C := by
  sorry

end Erdos1159

reformulations.difference: The source asks for an absolute constant C > 1 (a real constant) such that every finite projective plane has a set S of points with 1 ≤ |S ∩ ℓ| ≤ C for all lines ℓ. The Lean differs in form in four ways. (1) It takes `C : ℕ` with the side condition `1 < C`. (2) It quantifies over finite projective planes as Mathlib's `Configuration.ProjectivePlane P L`, with `P L : Type`, `Fintype` on both points and lines, and an arbitrary incidence relation `Membership P L` passed as an explicit binder. (3) It states "S meets ℓ" as `1 ≤ (S ∩ {p | p ∈ l}).ncard`. (4) It has no "sufficiently large order" qualifier.
reformulations.equivalence_argument:
(1) The condition `ncard ≤ C` is monotone in C. A real constant C can therefore be replaced by the natural number ⌈C⌉₊ + 2, which is > 1, and conversely. The side condition `1 < C` is harmless anyway: C = 0 is impossible, and so is C = 1, since a set meeting every line exactly once is a single point, and lines not through that point miss it.

(3) `P` is finite, so `ncard` is the true cardinality, and `1 ≤ ncard` is equivalent to nonemptiness.

I proved `RHS ↔ ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ (P L : Type) …, ∃ S, ∀ l, (S ∩ {p | p ∈ l}).Nonempty ∧ ((S ∩ {p | p ∈ l}).ncard : ℝ) ≤ C` in a scratch file (compiles). With `pp.explicit` I checked that `ProjectivePlane P L` and `p ∈ l` use the same bound `Membership` instance.

(2) Mathlib's `ProjectivePlane` (Nondegenerate + HasPoints + HasLines + `exists_config`) with finiteness is exactly a nondegenerate finite projective plane of order ≥ 2 (`one_lt_order`). `exists_config` rules out near-pencils. Restricting to `Type` loses nothing, because any finite plane transports along `Fintype.equivFin` to one on `Fin n`. The quantified class is non-empty: I built a `ProjectivePlane` on ℙ(ZMod 3)³ with `Fintype` instances in Lean.

(4) For one fixed plane the claim is trivial: S = all points gives C = order + 1 (proved in Lean). So all the content is in the uniform constant, exactly as in the source. For the same reason, a "sufficiently large order" variant is equivalent: planes of order < N are handled by S = all points with C = N.

review.notes:
What the sources pose.
- The erdosproblems.com LaTeX source reads: "Determine whether there exists a constant $C>1$ such that the following holds. Let $P$ be a finite projective plane. Must there exist a set of points $S$ such that $1\leq \lvert S\cap \ell\rvert \leq C$ for all lines $\ell$?" The theorem docstring reproduces this word for word.
- The page's references match the module docstring.
- The primary source [Er81, p. 12, problem 1] asks: "Is there an absolute constant C so that every finite plane has a blocking set which meets every line but each in at most C points?"
- Asgarli–Ghioca–Yip (arXiv 2510.15332) state it as: is k(n) bounded, where k(n) is the least k such that every projective plane of order n has a blocking set B with |B∩L| < k for all L.
- The Lean `answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ C : ℕ, 1 < C ∧ ∀ finite projective planes, ∃ S, ∀ l, 1 ≤ |S ∩ l| ≤ C` matches all three. The quantifier order is right: C comes before the plane, and S depends on the plane. The polarity is positive, so this is not a negated conjecture.

Why "blocking set" means any set meeting every line. The Lean does not require S to avoid containing a whole line. That is correct. The site defines "A set which meets all lines at once is called a blocking set", and so does the arXiv paper. If nontriviality were required, the question would be trivially false: the Fano plane has no nontrivial blocking set.

Status. The source still records the problem as open, consistent with `research open`:
- erdosproblems.com shows OPEN (page last edited 10 April 2026; the only edit since creation added the Green's-list sentence).
- teorth/erdosproblems lists it as open (2026-01-23).
- Asgarli–Ghioca–Yip (Oct 2025) call it "still wide open".
- Green's list gives the PG(2,q) special case and says it is speculated to fail for large primes q.
- Erdős 664 (the stronger family version, disproved by Alon using subsets of lines) does not settle it.

Out of scope for this file. The [Er81] generalisation to pairwise balanced block designs is formalised elsewhere, as `Erdos664.variants.block_design`; its absence here is not a defect.

Access limits. erdosproblems.com blocks curl with a Cloudflare challenge, so I read it through the r.jina.ai reader proxy. [ESS83] is an image-only scan, so its content comes from the erdosproblems.com remarks and the arXiv paper's summary; the formal statement does not depend on it.
